deep.reconstruction:
Title: 'Shortest line (geodesic) on the spheroid'. Setup: ζ is the azimuth, counted from north through east. φ is geodetic latitude and λ is longitude. The equatorial radius is 1, although Gauss later reinstates a factor a in ds. e is the eccentricity and W = sqrt(1-e^2 sin^2 φ).

(1) Clairaut's integral. cos φ sin ζ / W = cos J is constant along the geodesic. Here cos φ/W is the distance from the axis; this is Clairaut's relation r sin ζ = const.
[Mine:] Introduce the reduced latitude β with tan β = sqrt(1-e^2) tan φ, so that cos β = cos φ/W. Then cos J = cos β sin ζ. On the Bessel-type auxiliary sphere (latitude β), J is the inclination of the image great circle to the equator, and J is the maximum reduced latitude.

(2) Auxiliary quantities.
- tan i = tan J / sqrt(1-e^2). So i is the geodetic latitude whose reduced latitude is J, i.e. the vertex (maximum) geodetic latitude.
- tan φ / tan i = sin P, which equals tan β / tan J. By Napier's rule for the right triangle node–point–foot, P is the spherical longitude measured from the node (Bessel's ω).
- cos P sin J = cos ζ. This is Napier again: the spherical azimuth equals the ellipsoidal azimuth ζ.
- cos P sin i = cos R. This defines a second auxiliary sphere: a great circle of inclination i, which at longitude P has latitude ψ with tan ψ = tan i sin P = tan φ, i.e. it carries the geodetic latitude φ itself. R is the azimuth there.
- [Mine:] cos R / cos ζ = sin i / sin J = 1/sqrt(1-e^2 cos^2 J) =: k, which is constant. One also has 1-e^2 sin^2 i = (1-e^2) k^2. Differentiating gives dζ = dR sqrt(1-e^2)/W, as written. The next page gives the equivalent tan R = tan ζ sqrt(1-e^2)/W.

(3) Differential relations.
- dλ = dP sqrt((1-e^2)/W^2). This is Bessel's dλ = sqrt(1-e^2 cos^2 β) dω, since 1-e^2 cos^2 β = (1-e^2)/W^2.
- dζ = dP sin φ sqrt(1-e^2)/W. This equals sin β dP (great-circle azimuth change) and also sin φ dλ (ellipsoid geodesic). It is also consistent with dR = sin φ dP on the second sphere.
- ds = a dQ (1-e^2)/(sqrt(1-e^2 cos^2 J) W^3) = a dQ sqrt(1-e^2 sin^2 i) sqrt(1-e^2)/W^3. Here Q is the arc on the second sphere.
- [Mine:] Derivation of ds: dφ = dQ cos R on the second sphere, and dφ = ds cos ζ W^3/(a(1-e^2)) on the ellipsoid. Hence ds = M k dQ, where M is the meridian radius of curvature. The next page writes this as dQ = A^3 ds/B.

(4) Comparison curve: the normal section. Take the plane containing the surface normal at (λ=0, φ0) with azimuth ζ0. The surface point is X = cos φ cos λ/W, Y = cos φ sin λ/W, Z = (1-e^2) sin φ/W.
[Mine:] The plane normal is m = -cos ζ0 (0,1,0) + sin ζ0 (-sin φ0, 0, cos φ0). Imposing m·(X - X0) = 0 and dividing by -sin ζ0 gives Gauss's condition:
sin φ0 X + cot ζ0 Y - cos φ0 Z = e^2 sin φ0 cos φ0 / W0.
Multiplying by W gives the 'simpler' form, with right side e^2 cos φ0 sin φ0 sqrt(W^2/W0^2). Gauss first wrote e^2 cos φ sin φ and corrected it.

Purpose: to set up the geodesic via auxiliary-sphere parametrisations (P, Q, R) and to compare the geodesic with the normal section through a point.
errors: No mathematical errors found; every relation was verified.
Minor inconsistency: the equatorial radius is set to 1, yet ds carries a factor a.
The cancelled first right-hand side of the last equation (ee cos φ sin φ) was correctly replaced by ee cos φ0 sin φ0.

results.what: cos φ sin ζ / sqrt(1-e^2 sin^2 φ) = const along a geodesic
Mapping the geodesic to a great circle on an auxiliary sphere with reduced latitude: tan β = tan J sin P, cos ζ = cos P sin J, dλ = sqrt(1-e^2 cos^2 β) dP, dζ = sin β dP
results.modern_name: Auxiliary sphere method for ellipsoidal geodesics (Bessel's method)

results.what: Second auxiliary sphere carrying geodetic latitude: cos R = cos P sin i, tan R = tan ζ sqrt(1-e^2)/W, ds = M dQ / sqrt(1-e^2 cos^2 J)
results.usually_credited_to: unsure (a variant of the Legendre/Bessel approach)

results.what: Equation of the normal section through (0, φ0) with azimuth ζ0 in geodetic coordinates

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard geodesic theory on the spheroid (Clairaut plus auxiliary sphere). The pencil note 'Band IX S. 74' indicates the page was printed in Gauss's Werke IX, so it is already known. The second auxiliary sphere is a mildly non-standard but equivalent variant.

1-e^2 sin^2 i = (1-e^2) k^2, which links the two ds forms; should give 0
dλ = dP sqrt((1-e^2)/W^2) agrees with Bessel's dλ = sqrt(1-e^2 cos^2 β) dω; should give 0
dζ = sin β dP equals sin φ sqrt(1-e^2)/W dP; should give 0

checkable.sympy: e,f,f0,l,z0=symbols('e phi phi0 lam zeta0'); W=sqrt(1-e**2*sin(f)**2); W0=sqrt(1-e**2*sin(f0)**2); X=cos(f)*cos(l)/W; Y=cos(f)*sin(l)/W; Z=(1-e**2)*sin(f)/W; simplify((sin(f0)*X+cot(z0)*Y-cos(f0)*Z - e**2*sin(f0)*cos(f0)/W0).subs({l:0,f:f0}))
checkable.asserts: The normal-section plane passes through the point (0, φ0); should give 0

checkable.sympy: e,f0,z0=symbols('e phi0 zeta0'); n0=Matrix([cos(f0),0,sin(f0)]); t=cos(z0)*Matrix([-sin(f0),0,cos(f0)])+sin(z0)*Matrix([0,1,0]); m=Matrix([sin(f0),cot(z0),-cos(f0)]); simplify(m.dot(n0)), simplify(m.dot(t))
checkable.asserts: The plane normal (sin φ0, cot ζ0, -cos φ0) is orthogonal to the surface normal and to the azimuth-ζ0 tangent; both should give 0

transcription_corrections: The second ds expression ends at the page edge as 'sqrt(1-ee sin i^2) sqrt(1-ee)'; the second root is cut off but must be sqrt(1-ee), which is consistent with the mathematics.
Pencil archival note near the title reads 'Band IX S. 74' (Werke IX, p. 74), and the upper-left pencil reads 'Geodätisch' / 'Kr'; the transcription omits these.
In the line 'cos P sin i = cos R' the R is written as a large calligraphic R; it is the same R as in ∂ζ = ∂R sqrt(1-ee)/sqrt(1-ee sin φ^2).
